messages.content: You design amateur rockets that fly on certified commercial motors. Work through the design, check it with the tools, and give the final design as JSON inside <design> tags. Only report results the tools returned.
Need a hand. Two-stage rocket: Cesaroni O3400 booster, Cesaroni M2045 sustainer. It needs to break 7,500 m. Each piece that separates must land under 6 m/s. Any ideas?

messages.reasoning_content:
1. Understand: two stages with the motors fixed. Booster is a Cesaroni O3400. Sustainer is a Cesaroni M2045. Apogee is a minimum of 7,500 m. Each piece that separates has to land at or under 6 m/s, so both stages need their own chute. Rail and wind are not given, so I assume a 1.5 m rail and 2 m/s wind. Vertical, sea level.
2. Feasibility: a drag-free coast to 7,500 m needs sqrt(2 * 9.81 * 7500) = 384 m/s after the upper burn. An O under an M should have the impulse if the airframe is not absurdly heavy. Both motors are large, so the chutes will be large too. I need diameters, masses, and thrust before drawing tubes.

2. Feasibility: O3400 comes back as 21062O3400-P, 21041 N*s, 3421 N, 98 mm by 1.239 m, 16.8 kg loaded. M2045 comes back as 7388M2045-P, 7327.6 N*s, 2084 N, 75 mm by 0.893 m, 6.07 kg loaded. 21041 + 7327.6 = 28400 N*s combined, under the 40,960 N*s cap. Both delays are only 0 s, so the motors stay plugged and the chutes are electronic. A 98 mm motor does not fit in a 98 mm tube, so the airframe is 112 mm. Guessed liftoff mass 35 kg. Thrust-to-weight is 3421 / (35 * 9.81) = 10. Rail acceleration is (3421 - 35 * 9.81) / 35 = 88 m/s^2, so rail exit is sqrt(2 * 88 * 1.5) = 16 m/s, just over 15. The altitude minimum looks reachable.
3. Size: the sustainer flies alone with the M in its tail, so its fins have to be large or it tumbles at ignition. Those fins also sit forward on the stack and pull the combined CP forward, so the booster fins have to be larger still or the launch margin goes negative. Sustainer descent mass is about 8 kg. At 5 m/s and Cd 0.8 the area is 2 * 8 * 9.81 / (1.225 * 0.8 * 5^2) = 6.4 m^2, diameter sqrt(4 * 6.4 / 3.1416) = 2.9 m. I'll fit 2.8 m. Booster descent mass is about 12 kg, area 2 * 12 * 9.81 / (1.225 * 0.8 * 5^2) = 9.6 m^2, diameter sqrt(4 * 9.6 / 3.1416) = 3.5 m. I'll fit 3.8 m so the heavier piece has margin under 6 m/s. Separate at booster burnout and light the M immediately.
4. Draft: 112 mm fiberglass. Sustainer on top, four fins with 0.22 m span, 2.8 m chute at apogee, M2045 plugged. Booster below, four fins with 0.32 m span, 3.8 m chute at its own apogee, O3400 plugged. Checking the stack.

messages.reasoning_content:
4. Check: the simulator gives apogee 7763.8 m, above the 7,500 m minimum. Rail-exit margin is 1.94 cal and the burn minimum is 1.94 cal, both above 1.0. Rail exit is 18.9 m/s and thrust-to-weight is 9.6. The booster reached the ground at 4.8 m/s with its chute open. The sustainer chute opened at 33.1 s and the descent rate is 5.2 m/s, under 6. The run stopped at 1199.6 s with the sustainer still airborne, which is the long fall from 7763.8 m, not a failed recovery. Both sections have recovery deployed. Every scored check passes.
5. Fix: no fix was needed.
6. Uncertainty: max Mach is 2.12 and the tool warns that body drag is unreliable above Mach 1, so the apogee can move. The sustainer number 5.2 m/s is the descent rate when the run hit its time limit, not an impact. Chute Cd is a model 0.8. Liftoff mass is 36.3 kg, and 18.9 - 15 = 3.9 m/s is all the rail spare there is. The open-airframe warning is the booster tube after it separates.

Launch margin is 1.94 cal. The sustainer was still in the air when the run reached its time limit.
